edges.description: Loss of tyrosine aminotransferase activity prevents normal tyrosine degradation, causing tyrosine to accumulate in blood and tissues.
Elevated intracellular tyrosine deposits in the cornea and in palmoplantar epidermis, triggering the inflammatory and hyperkeratotic tissue response.
Sustained hypertyrosinemia, particularly when diagnosis is delayed or treatment is lacking, is associated with variable neurodevelopmental impairment.
intermediate_mechanisms: central-nervous-system effects of chronic tyrosine elevation

edges.description: Corneal tyrosine deposition drives an inflammatory pseudodendritic keratitis.
Epidermal tyrosine deposition in the palms and soles produces painful focal hyperkeratosis.

nodes.description: The upstream enzymatic block produces marked hypertyrosinemia. Unlike tyrosinemia type I, no downstream hepatotoxic metabolites (fumarylacetoacetate, succinylacetone) are generated; tyrosine itself is the accumulating and pathogenic metabolite, deposited intracellularly in the cornea and in the epidermis of the palms and soles.

evidence.reference_title: Richner-Hanhart syndrome (tyrosinemia type II): a case report of delayed diagnosis with pseudodendritic corneal lesion.
evidence.snippet: Blood tests showed a tyrosine level of 508 micromol/L (normal range: 30-150).

nodes.description: Variable intellectual disability, more likely with delayed diagnosis or untreated disease.

evidence.snippet: Tyrosinemia type II is characterized by corneal dystrophy, painful palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and variable intellectual disability.

nodes.description: Painful, bilateral, often pseudodendritic (herpetiform) keratitis presenting with photophobia and tearing, characteristically unresponsive to antiviral therapy and improving with tyrosine-lowering diet.

evidence.reference_title: Point mutations in the tyrosine aminotransferase gene in tyrosinemia type II.
evidence.snippet: characterized by keratitis, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, mental retardation, and elevated blood tyrosine levels.

nodes.description: Intracellular tyrosine crystal deposition in the corneal epithelium provokes a pseudodendritic, herpetiform keratitis with corneal dystrophy that is characteristically unresponsive to antiviral therapy, while deposition in palmoplantar epidermis produces painful focal hyperkeratosis.

evidence.reference_title: Richner-Hanhart syndrome (tyrosinemia type II): a case report of delayed diagnosis with pseudodendritic corneal lesion.
evidence.snippet: Biomicroscopic examination revealed bilateral circular corneal opacities on the inferior quadrant and small dendritic lesions at the center of the circular opacities.

evidence.reference_title: Richner-Hanhart syndrome (tyrosinemia type II): a case report of delayed diagnosis with pseudodendritic corneal lesion.
evidence.snippet: Tyrosinemia type II should be suspected in patients demonstrating dermatologic signs, especially palmoplantar keratosis, associated with bilateral pseudodendritic corneal lesions unresponsive to antiviral therapy.

nodes.description: Painful focal hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles.

evidence.snippet: Tyrosinemia type II is characterized by corneal dystrophy, painful palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and variable intellectual disability.

evidence.reference_title: Point mutations in the tyrosine aminotransferase gene in tyrosinemia type II.
evidence.snippet: The disease results from deficiency in hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT; L-tyrosine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, EC 2.6.1.5), a 454-amino acid protein encoded by a gene with 12 exons.

evidence.reference_title: Point mutations in the tyrosine aminotransferase gene in tyrosinemia type II.
evidence.snippet: DNA sequence analysis of the regions identified as nonfunctional revealed six different point mutations.

nodes.description: Nonsense, missense, and splice-site point mutations in TAT abolish tyrosine aminotransferase activity; nonsense mutations at codons 57, 223, and 417 and splice-donor/acceptor mutations were among the first characterized.

Biallelic loss-of-function TAT variants reduce hepatic cytosolic tyrosine aminotransferase activity, blocking the first (transamination) step of tyrosine catabolism that converts L-tyrosine to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate.

evidence.reference_title: Point mutations in the tyrosine aminotransferase gene in tyrosinemia type II.
evidence.snippet: The disease results from deficiency in hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT; L-tyrosine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, EC 2.6.1.5), a 454-amino acid protein encoded by a gene with 12 exons.
The diagnosis of tyrosinemia type II is established in a proband by identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in TAT on molecular genetic testing
